author: Native News Online Staff
title: Navajo Nation Supreme Court Denies Petition Challenging Budget and Finance Committee Investigation
content:
The Navajo Nation Supreme Court has denied a petition seeking extraordinary relief related to an ongoing investigation by the Navajo Nation Council’s Budget and Finance Committee into housing and related matters.

The Supreme Court denied the Navajo Nation Assistant Attorneys General’s Petition for Writ of Certiorari or Clarifying Opinion on procedural grounds. The petition sought review of an order issued by the Window Rock District Court in Cause No. WR-CV-49-26 concerning the validity of legislative subpoenas issued as part of the Budget and Finance Committee’s investigation.

The Assistant Attorneys General did not attach a copy of the district court’s order to their petition, as required by the Supreme Court’s rules of procedure.

The Supreme Court therefore did not address the underlying issues raised in the district court order.

The petition followed the Window Rock District Court’s June 18, 2026, dismissal of a Petition for Extraordinary Writ filed by the Assistant Attorneys General. That petition raised questions concerning subpoenas issued to witnesses expected to testify before the Budget and Finance Committee.

author: By Elyse Wild
title: Federal Food Officials Want to Know When Companies Add New Chemical Ingredients to American Diets
content:
Food manufacturers may have to start disclosing to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration the ingredients they determine to be safe for consumption, according to an announcement made today by the Department of Health and Human Services.

A new rule proposed by federal food regulators could begin to close a loophole that allows food manufacturers to determine, with no FDA oversight or required disclosure, that an ingredient is safe to add to food products.

The Red 40 that gives Flamin’ Hot Cheetos the color that stains fingers is a chemical ingredient that food makers determined safe to eat under federal food safety standards established in 1958.

Those standards put the responsibility on food manufacturers to test and verify the safety of any new chemical ingredients. U.S. companies have been allowed to determine on their own if substances added to their products are Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS), without notifying the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. GRAS denotes that qualified experts agree that an ingredient is not harmful to consume under its intended uses.

With companies in control, this has resulted in thousands of unknown chemical additives in food that have led to a wide range of health complications.

author: Levi Rickert
title: Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation Celebrates Opening of Its Field Museum “#Land Band” Exhibition
content:
CHICAGO — Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation Tribal Chairman Joseph “Zeke” Rupnick recalled how the Potawatomi were once labeled “combatant enemies of the government” during the forced removals of the 1830s, when the Tribe was driven from Illinois to present-day Kansas and Oklahoma.

Rupnick made the remarks Tuesday during the opening of his Tribe’s #LandBack exhibition, part of the Native Truths: Our Voices, Our Stories exhibit at the Field Museum in Chicago.

The new installation comes more than two years after Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker signed legislation in March 2024 transferring an entire state park in southern DeKalb County to the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, restoring a portion of its ancestral homeland. Less than a month later, on April 19, 2024, the U.S. Department of the Interior placed portions of the historic Shab-eh-nay Reservation into trust for the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, making it the only federally recognized tribal nation with trust land in Illinois.

Joining Rupnick at the exhibition opening were Prairie Band Potawatomi Tribal Council members Raphael Wahwassuck and Ronald “Tony” Wahweotten Jr., representing the Nation at the historic event.

Rupnick traced the history of the Potawatomi removal from Illinois in the 1830s when they were forcibly removed from their ancestral homelands and compelled to cede nearly 28 million acres in the Great Lakes region

author: Native News Online Staff
title: UN to Mark International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples With Focus on Indigenous Midwives
content:
The United Nations will mark the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples on Monday, August 10, with a virtual commemoration highlighting the vital role Indigenous midwives play in safeguarding the health, well-being and cultural continuity of their communities.

The 2026 theme is “Honouring Indigenous Midwives: Safeguarding Life and Well-being.”

The International Day is officially observed each year on August 9. In 1994, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 49/214 establishing August 9 as the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples. The date commemorates the first meeting of the United Nations Working Group on Indigenous Populations, held in 1982.

Because August 9 falls on a Sunday this year, the UN’s virtual commemoration will be held Monday, August 10.

The event will take place from 8:30 to 10:30 a.m. EDT (New York time).

The virtual program will begin with an Indigenous spiritual ceremony, followed by statements from senior United Nations officials and the chair of the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues.

Two moderated dialogues will then focus on Indigenous midwifery, traditional knowledge and the need for greater recognition and support.

author: Shaun Griswold
title: On The Corn Pollen Trail With Deb Haaland
content:
In the morning , before sunrise, I pray with corn pollen in my right hand. The corn was harvested from red clay soil in the fields of the Zuni Mountains, where my Pueblo relatives live and pray in the same way. At an early age, I was taught that a corn-pollen prayer centers the belief that a person is exactly where they’re supposed to be at any given time and place, creating a presence with all existence that is determined by the prayer itself. Land-based belief systems exist across the world, and this one, which is practiced in my Southwestern home, respects the notion that life is a constant path forward, and therefore you must set your path. Facing east toward the Sandia Mountains, I speak my gratitude for the morning and offer peaceful intentions for my day. I thank my grandparents and acknowledge their ancestors and the younger ancestors I knew and loved who are no longer in this moment to breathe the morning air with me. I toss the corn pollen at my feet, just as my relatives have done before me and like everyone who comes after me will do. We have done this since, well, forever.

This article first appeared on High Country News and is republished here with permission.

author: By B. 'Toastie' Oaster
title: Tribally Contested Badger Mountain Solar Project Canceled By Developer
content:
Energy developer Avangrid withdrew last month its longstanding permit application to build industrial-scale solar on a site sacred to the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation and the Confederated Tribes and bands of the Yakama Nation. The proposed project site on Badger Mountain in central Washington straddles private land as well as public land owned by the Washington Department of Natural Resources. Tribal nations have the right to practice cultural traditions, such as food gathering and ceremony, on public lands, and a 2024 investigation by HCN and ProPublica revealed that Avangrid’s proposed solar development threatened those rights.

This article first appeared on High Country News and is republished here with permission.

“The Colville Tribes is very happy to hear that the proposed solar project on Badger Mountain has been withdrawn,” said Chairwoman Cindy Marchand in an emailed statement last week. “While the Colville Tribes certainly appreciates the value of renewable energy such as solar power, sacred sites must remain pristine to pass down to future generations. We appreciate Avangrid Power LLC’s decision to withdraw this project and we trust that they can find a more appropriate site.”

author: Elyse Wild
title: Chickasaw Nation Breaks Ground on One of Country’s Largest Native American Hospitals
content:
Last week, Chickasaw Nation broke ground on what will be one of the largest Native American hospitals in the country.

When complete, the 160-acre Chickasaw Nation Health Newcastle Medical Center campus, located at the intersection of Southwest 16th Street and U.S. Highway 62, will contain 12 buildings, including a hospital, outpatient clinic, and more than 23 medical specialties.

“Today is the next step in our journey to provide quality, accessible healthcare,” Chickasaw Nation Governor Chris Anoatubby said at the July 31 groundbreaking ceremony. “This will be more than just a hospital; this campus will propel healthcare forward.”

In Oklahoma, Native adults have some of the highest rates of some chronic diseases, including type 2 diabetes, cancers, and heart disease. Those disparities are in step with the rest of Indian Country, and with the Indian Health Service (IHS) struggling under a budget shortfall of tens of billions of dollars , tribes like Chickasaw Nation are taking healthcare into their own hands.

“Once again, the mission extends to the community and other First Americans we will serve right here in Newcastle. author: Professor Victoria Sutton
title: Peptides Find Their Way to the Public
content:
Guest Opinion

The FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee met on Thursday and Friday, July 23-24, 2026, convening to consider whether seven peptides should be be made more widely available. Six of the seven received a green light, so to speak.

This committee is subject to the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), which requires its members to be non-federal employees. Its meetings must be open to the press, and its documents are subject to the Freedom of Information Act. It is a standard way for the federal government to conduct business when outside professional and expert opinions are needed, although the committee’s recommendations are advisory only.

A Very Brief History of the FDCA

The Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 was enacted in response to public outrage over food tampering and hidden ingredients in drugs, such as opium and alcohol, but perhaps was driven most by the reaction to Upton Sinclair’s book The Jungle . Although the book was intended to expose the poor working conditions of immigrants, its depiction of shocking food processing and canning practices in Chicago instead sparked widespread concern about food safety.

The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act was enacted in 1938 to protect the public from adulterated or misbranded foods, drugs, devices, and cosmetics after a poisoning incident involving an antibiotic that killed 100 people.

author: Elyse Wild
title: As Screens Take Over, Advocates Say Play, Culture Are Key to Native Youth Mental Health
content:
The answer to a growing mental health crisis in a world in which screens are omnipresent and social media is fueling a sense of despair among the nation’s young people may be simple: get outside and play.

That’s according to a new report by Kaboom!, a nonprofit that builds playgrounds around the nation. The report was created in collaboration with IndigiFit Kids , a three-year campaign by the Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community aimed at improving the physical and mental health of Native youth in Minnesota.

The report outlines data that shows mental health among the nation’s young people is plummeting, and Native youth are the most at risk. Increased screen time, reduced physical activity, slashed recess times, and more than 28 million kids lacking access to a green space or playground point to a shrinking childhood. From 2017 to 2021, depression diagnoses among children rose by 60%, with anxiety rising by 31%. While the issue touches every community, Native communities bear the brunt: suicide rates among Native youth ages 15 to 19 are double that of white youth. But among the bleak numbers, there is hope: kids who spend 60 minutes a day in nature have a 50% lower risk of mental health issues.
